title: Sidewall-printed vertical buses replace TSVs in offset die stacks
idea: Scarcity: TSVs banned. Stack thinned DRAM dies with a 20 um staircase offset so every die exposes an edge pad row, then aerosol-jet print 10 um copper/silver traces down the stepped sidewall (with printed polymer dielectric between traces) to tie every tier to the base die.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV keep-out area and TSV-driven 20-30% yield loss, recovering ~25-30% of die area per bit; printing tools are cheap and U.S.-available.

title: Retired LCD fab lines reborn as panel-level memory interposer foundries
idea: Scarcity: CoWoS silicon interposer capacity is sold out. Retool depreciated Gen-6/Gen-8 TFT-LCD lines (1.5-2 um steppers, large-area sputter and CVD already installed) to pattern copper RDL interposers on 1.5 m glass panels, cutting ~100 interposers per panel instead of ~15 per 300 mm wafer.
why: Capital intensity and the HBM packaging chokepoint: fully depreciated tools and ~5-8x more interposer area per exposure, targeting 3-5x lower $/mm2 of interposer.

title: Resonant LC tank bus recycles signal charge between complementary wires
idea: Scarcity: the whole link gets 1 pJ/bit. Pair each data wire with its complement through an on-package thin-film inductor so a transition sloshes charge from one line to the other at LC resonance (adiabatic signaling) instead of dumping CV2 to ground; drivers only top up resistive loss.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): recovering ~70-80% of line charge targets <1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM and 10-20 pJ/bit DDR5.

title: Traversal descriptors replace command-address pins entirely
idea: Scarcity: zero command/address pins. The host writes a compact traversal program (base, strides, gather-index pointer, tile shape) into a sequencer in the memory base die once; memory then streams data in consumption order with only a 1-bit flow-control backchannel.
why: Frees ~25-30% of interface pins for data and removes CA energy; the sequencer sees the whole access pattern and orders activations to cut fact-8 page overfetch 2-4x on tensor workloads.

title: Wavelength is the address: bank-per-color photonic interposer
idea: Scarcity: no address decode logic on the memory die. A silicon-nitride photonic interposer gives each DRAM bank a fixed WDM wavelength via a tuned microring drop filter; a request is a pulse on that bank's color and the reply returns on the same color, so routing and arbitration happen optically.
why: Cuts address/command periphery (fact 7) and long electrical routes (fact 5); 32-64 wavelengths x 25 Gb/s per waveguide targets ~1-2 pJ/bit at cm reach.

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops DRAM dies into hybrid-bond sites
idea: Scarcity: die bonders are the bottleneck tool. Dies with a keyed outline and hydrophobic backside are tumbled in a carrier liquid over a logic wafer with matching hydrophilic recesses; capillary forces self-align them to <0.5 um and the wafer is batch-annealed into Cu-Cu hybrid bonds.
why: Packaging capital intensity: replaces ~1,000 dies/hr pick-and-place with wafer-parallel placement (1e4-1e5 dies/hr per tank), ~10x less bonding capex per stack.

title: Diamond via-layer lets DRAM sit directly atop hot GPU logic
idea: Scarcity: memory may not exceed 85 C yet must sit within 50 um of compute. A 20-50 um CVD-diamond interlayer (k~1,500 W/mK) with laser-drilled copper vias at 10 um pitch sits between GPU and hybrid-bonded DRAM, spreading hotspots sideways to edge cold plates before heat reaches the DRAM.
why: Data movement (fact 5): vertical DRAM-on-logic drops ~3-4 pJ/bit HBM traffic to ~0.2-0.5 pJ/bit by deleting the interposer trip; diamond makes the thermal stack survivable.

title: Array-only DRAM wafer bonded to periphery wafer at subarray IO
idea: Scarcity: the DRAM die may contain zero periphery. Build a wafer of only cell mats plus local sense amps, expose each subarray's local I/O lines and wordline-driver inputs as ~0.5 um-pitch hybrid-bond pads, and bond it face-to-face to a cheap logic wafer carrying decoders, column logic, DLL and I/O.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7): ~1.6-1.8x bits per DRAM wafer, and periphery moves to faster, cheaper logic with shorter on-die data paths.

title: Publish-subscribe row broadcast turns overfetch into delivered prefetch
idea: Scarcity: no fetched bit may be wasted. When a row opens, the base die multicasts the row's other lines on a low-priority channel to every last-level-cache slice that registered interest in that address region (a subscription table in the base die) instead of discarding them at precharge.
why: Fact 8 (128x overfetch, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit): converting even 10-20% of overfetched lines into hits cuts energy per useful bit ~2x on irregular workloads.

title: Layer-clocked just-in-time weight streaming caps HBM at 4 GB
idea: Scarcity: each accelerator gets only 4 GB of local DRAM. Since transformer layer order is deterministic, the compiler emits an exact transfer schedule so layer L+2's weights and KV blocks land from pooled far memory into a double-buffered ring exactly as layer L finishes.
why: Does DRAM's job with less: local HBM per accelerator drops 5-20x and far memory can be cheaper DDR/LPDDR, sidestepping HBM's ~3x wafer area per bit (fact 6).

title: Helium-free laser-etched vias for memory stacks
idea: Scarcity: no helium (Qatar offline), so no He backside-cooled DRIE chucks and no He leak tests. Form through-vias by femtosecond laser modification plus selective wet etching (laser-induced deep etching) in glass or silicon carriers, and check hermeticity with a hydrogen/forming-gas tracer.
why: Helium chokepoint and via cost: batch wet etch handles many wafers per bath with no plasma tool, removing helium from via formation.

title: Interlocking copper nanowire velcro makes cold-welded reworkable die joints
idea: Scarcity: no solder reflow and no bump pitch above 2 um. Template-electroplate dense 100 nm Cu nanowire forests on facing pads; pressing at room temperature interlocks and cold-welds them into 1-2 um-pitch joints that can be pulled apart and re-pressed.
why: HBM micro-bump pitch and yield (fact 6): no warpage from reflow, a bad die is reworked instead of scrapping the stack, and I/O density rises ~25x vs 10 um bumps.

title: Voltage-stacked DRAM tiers slash power bumps by four
idea: Scarcity: only 15% of bumps may carry power. Put 4 DRAM dies in series voltage domains (each floating 1.1 V above the one below on a 4.4 V rail) so one current flows through all tiers; small switched-capacitor balancers absorb mismatch and signals cross domains through capacitive level shifters.
why: Power uses over half of stack bumps/TSVs; series stacking cuts supply current 4x, freeing bumps for data and cutting IR drop, ~1.5x bandwidth per stack footprint.

title: Bit-plane sliced stacks make data movement proportional to precision
idea: Scarcity: no reading bits the model will not use. Each die in a 16-high stack holds one bit-plane (die 0 = sign/MSB) and the base die reassembles words, so an FP4 inference read activates only the top 4 dies while FP16 training reads all 16.
why: Data movement and activation energy (facts 5, 8): low-precision reads cost ~4x less energy and bandwidth with no reformatting of stored weights.

title: Shingled face-to-face die tiles talk by capacitive overlap
idea: Scarcity: no interposer and no substrate wiring between dies. Lay DRAM and logic dies like roof shingles, alternating face-up and face-down so each edge overlaps its neighbor by 1 mm; 20 um capacitive pads in the overlap couple data across a thin oxide gap.
why: Interposer cost and TSV tax: no wires or TSVs, ~1-2 Tb/s per mm of overlap at <0.5 pJ/bit near-field coupling; packaging becomes mechanical placement.

title: Delay-insensitive self-timed link deletes DRAM DLLs and training
idea: Scarcity: no forwarded clock and no DLL on the DRAM. Send data in a level-encoded dual-rail (1-of-4 transition) code so every symbol carries its own timing; the DRAM side drops DLL/PLL, link training and per-pin deskew.
why: Periphery and idle power (fact 7): DLLs and training logic burn mW per channel at idle; targets 20-30% lower I/O power and near-instant power-state exit.

title: Line-rate exponent-sharing and ANS codec inside the base die
idea: Scarcity: no redundant bit may cross the link. The HBM base die carries a block-floating-point repacker (shared exponent per 32 values) plus an asymmetric-numeral-systems entropy coder that losslessly compresses BF16/FP8 tensors at line rate; the GPU memory controller decodes.
why: Data movement (fact 5): BF16 exponents hold ~2.5 bits of entropy in 8, giving 1.3-1.6x effective bandwidth and capacity without touching cells.

title: Plastic sub-terahertz waveguide ribbons link memory without lasers
idea: Scarcity: no lasers, and copper cannot reach beyond 10 cm. 140-300 GHz CMOS transceivers couple into polymer dielectric waveguides (PTFE/HDPE ribbons) linking memory modules to processors over 0.1-2 m at 50-100 Gb/s per strand.
why: Disaggregation energy (fact 5): pooled memory at ~1-3 pJ/bit with plastic media and CMOS-only transceivers, no III-V lasers.

title: CDMA-coded shared vertical bus: eight dies talk on one wire
idea: Scarcity: only one-eighth of the normal TSV count is allowed. Each die spreads its data with an orthogonal Walsh code onto shared vertical wires, and the base die correlates to separate the simultaneous transmissions, trading symbol rate for wire count.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): 4-8x fewer TSVs cut keep-out area and TSV yield loss while keeping aggregate stack bandwidth.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pods exploit 77 K copper and leakage
idea: Scarcity: no new fabs, so wring more out of existing dies. Immerse memory sleds in LN2: at 77 K copper resistance falls ~7x, so buses run 3x longer at lower swing, and access-transistor leakage collapses so refresh nearly vanishes; cryocooler cost is shared across a rack.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and refresh (fact 3, 16-33% idle power): larger pooled memory per CPU at lower pJ/bit.

title: Approximate tensor lanes run 50 mV swing with no retries
idea: Scarcity: zero error-correction budget on the link. Tag activation and gradient traffic as approximate and run those lanes at ~50 mV swing and BER ~1e-6 with no ECC or retransmission, while pointers and metadata use standard robust lanes.
why: Interface energy and voltage floor (facts 5, 10): CV2 falls with swing, giving 3-5x lower I/O energy on most AI traffic.

title: Import known-good wafers, stack in America on open base die
idea: Scarcity: the U.S. has 1-2% of DRAM wafer capacity. Buy commodity DRAM wafers from any vendor under a wafer-level KGD spec, then do the high-value steps (thinning, hybrid bonding, a vendor-neutral base die from a U.S. logic foundry, final test) in U.S. OSATs.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: captures HBM value-add (~3-5x DDR $/bit) with ~$1-3B of packaging capex instead of a $15B fab.

title: Contactless inductive probing qualifies every die before stacking
idea: Scarcity: nothing may touch the die before bonding, since probe marks ruin hybrid-bond surfaces. Each die carries an on-die coil array and test controller; a coil probe card powers it inductively and runs full-speed tests wirelessly, so only pristine known-good dies enter the stack.
why: HBM yield loss (fact 6, 20-30%): stack yield is the product of die yields; complete KGD screening with no pad damage recovers most of it.

title: Bond-then-drill: one etch wires a 64-tier wafer stack
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Fusion-bond 64 DRAM wafers thinned to 5 um each (oxide bonding, <100 nm alignment), then pattern once and etch/fill vertical buses through the whole stack like a 3D-NAND channel hole, so one litho step and one deep etch replace 63 separate TSV and bump steps.
why: TSV/bump cost (fact 6) is amortized across tiers: 64 thin tiers vs 8-12 in HBM gives ~10x bits per footprint and volume while per-tier interconnect cost drops ~50x.

title: Porous-silicon release layers recycle donor wafers across forty tiers
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Build DRAM on a porous-silicon cleave layer (ELTRAN-style), transfer only the 2 um device film into the stack, then re-epi and reuse the donor substrate 10-20 times; 40+ films fit in the height of three normal dies.
why: Silicon and quartz-crucible chokepoint plus wafer cost: substrate cost per tier falls ~90%, paying for the extra tiers, so ~10x bits per footprint at similar package cost.

title: Infrared light shines straight through silicon to wire 100 tiers
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Silicon is transparent at 1310 nm, so a vertical beam from a VCSEL array under the stack passes through every thinned tier; each tier reads with a thin Ge photodiode and writes with a free-carrier-absorption modulator on the same spot, making optical vias with no drilling.
why: Deletes TSV process cost (fact 6) so tier count is limited only by thinning: 100 tiers of 10 um in 1 mm targets 10x bits per footprint at HBM-like package cost.

title: Roll memory like a film capacitor with sprayed end contacts
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Transfer DRAM device films onto a 10 um polyimide ribbon whose bus lines all exit at the two ribbon edges, wind it into a tight cylinder like a metallized-film capacitor, and arc-spray (Schoop) metal end caps that tie every turn's edge lines to power and a radial data comb.
why: Volumetric density with capacitor-industry roll-to-roll and winding tools that cost pennies per part; a 10 mm cylinder holds ~100x the silicon area of its footprint.

title: Bookshelf packaging stands DRAM dies on edge at 60 um pitch
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Route all die I/O to one edge, wafer-level plate that edge into contact fingers, and slot dies vertically like books into a glass rack whose floor carries the bus; no TSVs or stacking bonders, and coolant flows between the books.
why: Footprint density: a 10 x 10 mm rack holds ~150 standing dies vs 1 flat die, and edge plating is cheaper per die than TSV stacking.

title: Chip-on-glass display bonding builds memory cassettes for pennies
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Bond bare DRAM dies face-down onto 0.3 mm glass sheets with anisotropic conductive film exactly as LCD driver ICs are bonded (cents per bond, 1e5 bonds/day per line), then stack 20 sheets into a cassette with a flex edge connector.
why: Package substrate and socket cost (~$0.5-1 per die) disappears; sheets stack at ~0.4 mm pitch vs ~10 mm DIMM pitch, ~10x+ bits per volume at equal $/GB.

title: Passive optical splitter broadcasts one weight copy to sixteen accelerators
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Instead of every accelerator holding the full model, one memory node streams weights through a passive 1:16 optical star coupler while all 16 accelerators run the same layer in lockstep; each consumes the broadcast and keeps only activations and KV locally.
why: Duplicated weights fill much of fleet HBM; removing 15 of 16 copies raises effective capacity per purchased bit ~10x for inference, with splitters costing dollars.

title: Elastomeric zebra sheets make tall stacks solderless and rebuildable
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Stack 32-64 thinned dies interleaved with 30 um anisotropic conductive elastomer sheets (aligned metal filaments in silicone, as in LCD zebra connectors) under a clamped lid; a failed die is swapped by unclamping instead of scrapping the stack.
why: Tall-stack yield is multiplicative (fact 6); rework keeps stack yield near die yield, so 10x tiers cost ~10x dies with no yield penalty and no bonder capex.

title: Die-level erasure coding admits cheap downbinned dies into 48-high stacks
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Spread every cache line Reed-Solomon coded across 40 data dies plus 8 parity dies, with the base die mapping out dead banks, so dies with failed banks or weak cells (today scrapped or sold at 40-60% off) become first-class stack members.
why: Stack yield stops multiplying and discounted partial-good dies pay for the extra tiers: ~10x bits per package at the same package price.

title: Depreciated non-EUV fabs feed forty-tier capacity stacks
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Source 1x/2x-nm-class DRAM dies from fully depreciated, EUV-free lines (wafer cost ~1/3 of leading edge since depreciation is ~55% of cost) and stack 40 tiers per footprint so tiers, not lithography, deliver bits per mm2 of board.
why: Capital intensity and litho-bound scaling (fact 4): a node buys only 10-20% cost per bit, while 40 cheap tiers buy ~10x density per footprint at the same $/GB.

title: Undiced wafer-scale memory slabs with route-around redundancy
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Never dice the DRAM wafer: add a top metal mesh that routes around bad reticles, then mount whole 300 mm wafers as a stack of 10 slabs with edge connectors and liquid cooling between slabs.
why: Removes dicing, per-die packages, test sockets and module PCBs (~15-30% of module cost); a 10-wafer slab holds ~10x the bits per rack U of DIMMs at similar cost.

title: Defect-map matchmaking pairs wafers so tall W2W stacks still yield
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Keep a pool of thousands of probed DRAM wafers and run an assignment solver that stacks wafers whose bad die sites coincide (bad-on-bad), so defects concentrate in a few stack columns instead of poisoning many.
why: Wafer-on-wafer yield falls as y^N; matching can lift 32-high stack yield from ~20% to ~60% at typical defect densities, making 10x tiers affordable.

title: Urban-mined DRAM dies from retired servers restacked into dense modules
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Chemically decap DDR4 packages from decommissioned servers, retest the harvested dies, thin them and restack 16-32 high with wire-bond or sidewall interconnect into high-capacity modules for a capacity-tier memory product.
why: The dies are already paid for: near-zero die cost lets a module carry 10x the dies at the same price, made domestically from e-waste.

title: LED-strip memory tape spools gigabytes into empty chassis space
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Mount DRAM dies every 5 mm along a flat polyimide ribbon with a shared differential serial bus, built on reel-to-reel LED-strip SMT lines, and coil or fold the tape into chassis voids alongside cooling ducts.
why: Uses volume DIMM slots cannot reach at LED-strip assembly cost (fractions of a cent per placement): ~10x bits per chassis liter vs DIMMs.

title: Two-phase immersion memory bricks drop DIMM spacing to millimetres
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Mount dies on 0.2 mm boards at 1.5 mm pitch with boiling-channel gaps and submerge them in dielectric fluid; nucleate boiling removes ~100 W/cm2, so heat spreaders and airflow spacing disappear.
why: Volumetric density: air-cooled DIMM pitch is ~10 mm; 1.5 mm pitch gives ~6-10x bits per liter while dropping spreaders and fans offsets the fluid cost.

title: Inductively coupled tall stack wired only by two power bars
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Every tier talks to its neighbors through on-die coil pairs (no signal TSVs), and power enters through two thick copper bars plated into a single slot cut down the stack's side, so the only vertical metal in a 64-tier stack is power.
why: Removes signal TSVs and micro-bumps (fact 6) so interconnect cost no longer scales with tier count, enabling ~10x tiers per footprint at flat cost.

title: Base-die KV-cache codec stores ten contexts in one's space
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. The HBM base die compresses KV-cache blocks on write (per-channel 2-bit quantization, residual low-rank sketch, entropy-coded outliers) and decompresses on read at line rate, transparent to the GPU kernels.
why: KV cache dominates LLM serving memory; ~8-10x compression inside the module raises effective bits per purchased bit about 10x.

title: Seed-regenerated weights: memory interface synthesizes matrices from tiny seeds
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Store each weight block as a PRNG seed plus a few combination coefficients; an LFSR basis generator in the memory base die regenerates the block on the fly at read time, trading cheap logic gates for stored bits.
why: Capacity and data movement: ~8-12x fewer stored bits for weights, so ~10x model per GB of DRAM; logic gates cost far less than DRAM bits.

title: Alignment-free nanopillar film gives tenfold interconnect density
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. A directed-self-assembly block-copolymer membrane filled with 30 nm vertical copper pillars at 60 nm pitch joins any pad to the facing pad with no precision alignment, because every pad lands on hundreds of pillars.
why: Interconnect density: pads shrink from 9 um to ~1 um pitch without $5-10M hybrid-bond aligners, ~10-80x more vertical wires per mm2 at the same tool cost.

title: NAND-style zig-zag wire-bond stacks put 64 DRAM dies in one package
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Borrow mobile NAND packaging, where 16-32 dies stack in a zig-zag staircase with wire bonds for cents, and apply it to DRAM as a capacity tier: 64 dies per package on 8 wire-bonded channels at modest bandwidth.
why: Wire bonding is depreciated, U.S.-available and ~10x cheaper per die than TSV stacking; 64 dies per package is ~10x+ capacity per footprint vs 4-8-die DDR packages.

title: MicroLED mass-transfer stamps tile micro-chiplet DRAM in laminated layers
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Dice DRAM into 0.5 mm micro-chiplets and use microLED elastomer stamps to place 1e4 per stroke into a planarized polymer layer with printed RDL, repeating 10-20 layers like a PCB build-up.
why: Tiny chiplets yield ~99% and reclaim wafer-edge area, mass transfer cuts placement cost ~100x, and the layered build gives ~10x bits per footprint.

title: Vapor-chamber dies interleaved every eighth tier cool tall stacks
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Every eighth tier is a 50 um silicon vapor-chamber die (micro-wick etched into reclaimed wafers, water-filled, hermetically bonded) that carries heat sideways to the package edge, keeping 64-high stacks below 85 C.
why: Heat, not wiring, caps tall stacks; reclaimed-silicon cooling dies cost little, enable 10x tiers, and stop refresh rates (fact 3) from exploding.

title: Open tall-stack die standard turns memory dies into auctioned commodity
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. A JEDEC-style open spec fixes die size, thickness, pad maps and test interface for stackable DRAM dies so any vendor's dies drop into 32-64-high stacks; buyers reverse-auction dies and independent stackers compete separately.
why: Unbundling die-making from stacking lets tall stacks use the cheapest qualifying dies and opens many stacking houses (including U.S.), holding price flat at 10x dies per package.
